**Paragraph 1 — ATM:**
Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) is a connection-oriented network technology that operates by establishing virtual circuits before data transmission. All data is transmitted in fixed-size cells of exactly 53 bytes (5-byte header and 48-byte payload). ATM uses virtual path identifiers (VPIs) and virtual channel identifiers (VCIs) in its cell header to route cells along predetermined paths through the network, requiring explicit connection setup and teardown phases.

**Paragraph 2 — Ethernet:**
Ethernet is a connectionless network technology that operates on a best-effort model without requiring pre-established connections. Data is transmitted in variable-length frames, ranging from 64 to 1,518 bytes (standard Ethernet), with frame boundaries delimited by start and end markers. Ethernet uses MAC addresses in frame headers for forwarding decisions and allows multiple devices to share the same medium, with collisions handled through CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection) in half-duplex mode.

**Paragraph 3 — Carrying IP:**
The fundamental difference for IP transport is that ATM requires IP packets to be segmented into fixed 53-byte cells at the source and reassembled at the destination, introducing additional overhead and processing complexity. Ethernet, by contrast, encapsulates IP packets directly into variable-length frames, allowing IP packets to remain intact during transmission and simplifying handling at intermediate hops, making it more efficient for IP-centric networks.
